title: A new pipeline in an hour

beats.say: Why does starting a new data pipeline take six weeks in some companies?
Teams copy an old repository, file tickets for a schema, a connection and alerts, and wait. A template asks a few questions and creates a working repository in one step.
It asks only what it cannot guess: the product name, the domain, the owning team and the schedule. Everything else has a safe default.
The result runs on day one, with tests, alerts and an owner already in place.

check.q: What should a template ask the team?
opts: Only what it cannot infer, like name and owner
Every setting the pipeline could possibly use
Nothing at all; teams fill files in later
check.why: Few questions and safe defaults make the template fast and consistent.

work: Time how long your last new pipeline took to reach production.
List the questions a template would need to ask.

title: What a template creates

beats.say: What is inside a good data product template?
A standard layout, a pre-filled contract, a transformation project with one working example, and tests for the contract, data quality and code.
Then CI with policy checks, the orchestrator job as code with retries and alerts, monitors to the owner, catalog registration and a README.
Defaults matter most, because most teams keep them: retries, idempotent writes, a dead-letter table and schema checks.

show.title: Defaults teams keep
show.text:
retries: 3
write: overwrite_partition
dead_letter: true
schema_check: contract

check.q: Why do template defaults matter so much?
opts: Most teams keep them as they are
They are required by law in most places
They make the template much smaller
check.why: Defaults decide how most pipelines behave in production.

work: Write the defaults your template would set.
Check one of your pipelines against them.

title: Templates drift

beats.say: You fixed a bug in the template last month. Did the fix reach any of the teams that already used it?
A template is copied once. A year later, eighty repositories came from six versions, and last month's security fix reached none of them.
Version the template, record the version in each repository, and let a bot open upgrade pull requests with tests running.
Better still, copy less: shared CI and deployment workflows update everyone in one place.

check.q: What reaches every repository fastest with a fix?
opts: A shared workflow referenced by version
A copied file in each repository
An email asking teams to edit by hand
check.why: Shared workflows update in one place; copied files must be upgraded one by one.

work: Find which template versions your repositories are on.
Move one copied CI step into a shared workflow.

title: Choosing what to put in a template

beats.say: Should the template copy every file a team needs into the new repository, or should some parts live elsewhere?
Copy what each team will change: the contract, the model, the README. Reference what must change for everyone at once: CI, deployment, policy checks.
Every copied file is a file you will upgrade eighty times. Every referenced one is upgraded once.
Say this split out loud in a design interview: it shows you have run templates for years, not weeks.

check.q: Which part should a template reference rather than copy?
opts: The CI steps every team shares
The product's own contract file
The team's example data model
check.why: Shared steps change for everyone, so they belong in a versioned shared workflow.

work: Mark each file in your template as copy or reference.
Count the copied files you would have to upgrade.

title: Golden paths in one minute

beats.say: Thirty teams, thirty ways to build a pipeline. Is that a problem?
A golden path is the opinionated, supported way to do a common job, end to end. It bundles the decisions most teams should not have to make.
Three properties make it golden: it is the easiest way, it is supported by the platform team, and it is optional.
Teams may leave the path, but then they own what they build. Paths win by being better, not by being mandatory.

check.q: Which property is part of a golden path?
opts: Teams may leave it and own what they build
Every team must use it with no exceptions
Only the platform team is allowed to use it
check.why: Golden paths are optional; they win on speed and support.

work: Name one job your teams do thirty different ways.
Write what the golden way would be.

title: Which journeys to pave

beats.say: A platform team cannot pave every road at once. So which journeys should it pave first, and how does it decide?
List what teams do, how often, and how long it takes today. Pave the journeys that are both frequent and painful first.
Before building, shadow two teams doing the journey the hard way. Every wait and copy-paste goes on the backlog.
One or two journeys done really well beat ten journeys done badly and left to rot.

check.q: Which journey should usually be paved first?
opts: One done 20 times a quarter taking six weeks
One done twice a year taking two days
One that changes completely every month
check.why: Frequent and painful journeys repay the investment fastest.

work: List your teams' five most common journeys.
Write how often each happens and how long it takes.

title: Guardrails, not gates

beats.say: Should a review board approve every new pipeline?
A gate is a person who must approve. A guardrail is an automatic check that stops a mistake and says how to fix it, on every change.

show.title: Wait for a person, or *check in CI*

beats.say: Good guardrails: the contract exists and matches the data, personal data is masked, there is an owner, tests pass, costs stay in quota.
Every guardrail needs an escape hatch: a waiver with a reason, an owner and an expiry date.

check.q: What makes a waiver safe?
opts: It has an owner and an expiry date
It is approved once and kept forever
It is stored in a separate wiki page
check.why: An expiring waiver turns an exception into a dated decision.

work: Turn one manual review into a CI check.
Add expiry dates to every existing exception.

title: The developer portal

beats.say: Golden paths are useless if nobody can find them. Where do teams go to start something new?
A developer portal, often Backstage, brings together a catalog of everything, templates behind short forms, docs next to the code, and scorecards.
Scorecards show each component against the standards: owner, contract, tests passing, a supported template version, service levels met.
Do not let the portal and the data catalog compete. One place to start beats two half-complete ones.

check.q: What does a scorecard in a developer portal show?
opts: Each component against the standards
The salary bands of each team
Only the cost of the platform team
check.why: Scorecards make standards visible per component.

work: List the five checks your scorecard would show.
Decide whether portal or catalog is the front door.

title: Measuring a golden path

beats.say: The golden path exists and the template works. But is anyone choosing it, and is it saving them time?
Track adoption for new projects, time to first production run on and off the path, lead time and change failure rate, support tickets, and satisfaction.
If adoption is low, ask why before you mandate anything. Usually the path misses a real need, or it is slower than the old way.
Low adoption is a signal about the path, not about the teams.

check.q: Only 15% of new pipelines use the template. What first?
opts: Ask teams why they skipped it and fix that
Make the template mandatory right away
Build several more templates at once
check.why: Fix the reasons teams leave before mandating anything.

work: Compute adoption of your templates last quarter.
Interview one team that skipped the template.

title: How golden paths fail

beats.say: Most golden path programmes fail in the same few ways. Learn all of them before you build your first template.
A golden cage that cannot bend. Too many paths, none maintained. Stale templates nobody upgrades.
A path built without asking users. Gates disguised as paths, still ending in a ticket. Defaults nobody understands or can debug.
Each has a fix: escape hatches, fewer paths, upgrade bots, shadowing users, automatic guardrails, and docs.

check.q: The template still ends with a ticket to the platform team. What is this?
opts: A gate disguised as a golden path
A normal and healthy golden path
A golden cage with an escape hatch
check.why: Self-service means no waiting on a person for the common case.

work: Check your paths against the six failures.
Remove one ticket from your most used path.

title: Mandate the path or not?

beats.say: A director wants every team on the golden path by next quarter.
Agree with the goal, not the mandate. A mandate turns the path into a cage, and teams with real exceptions route around it.
Mandate the guardrails instead: owner, contract, masking and tests apply to everyone, on or off the path. Keep the path itself optional.
Then make the path the default in the portal, and retire support for the old ways with a date.

check.q: What should be mandatory for every team?
opts: The guardrails such as owner and masking
The template and the tools inside it
One orchestrator chosen by the director
check.why: Rules apply to all; the path stays optional and earns adoption.

work: Write which rules you would make mandatory.
Set a retirement date for one old way of working.

title: Owning a platform as a product

beats.say: Who owns the golden paths, and who pays?
The platform team owns the templates, the scaffolder, the shared workflows and the upgrade process, with a roadmap and support. Teams own what they create.
Do not build a path for a journey that happens twice a year, or for tools changing every month. Write a guide first, pave later.
Retire a path when its journey disappears, or wrap a managed service that does it better.

check.q: When should you write a guide instead of building a template?
opts: When the tools change every month
When thirty teams repeat the journey
When the journey takes six weeks today
check.why: A template for fast-moving tools is out of date in weeks; pave later.

work: Name the owner of each template you have.
Find one path you should retire.

title: Pave the busy, bumpy roads

beats.say: If you could pave only one road in a town, which would you pick?
Not the road nobody drives. Not the one that is already smooth. You pave the road where many people travel, and every trip is bumpy and slow.

chip.text: Pave where traffic and pain meet

beats.say: A data team is the same. Publishing a new data product happens twenty times a quarter and takes six weeks. That is a busy, bumpy road. Building a one-off feature table happens twice a quarter. A dirt track is fine there.

show.title: Count the trips
items: Publish a data product: 20 a quarter, 6 weeks
One-off feature table: 2 a quarter, 2 weeks
Pave the first, leave the second

beats.say: So you count the trips, time them, and pave the worst first. A few roads done well beat ten done badly.

check.q: Which journey is the best candidate for a paved path?
opts: One that happens often and takes teams a long time
One that is rare but very interesting to build
One that is already quick and has no waiting
One that the platform team finds easiest to build
check.why: Paving pays back when many people take the journey and each trip is slow. Rare, quick or merely convenient journeys do not repay the effort.

work: List the journeys your teams repeat most and write down how often each happens.
Ask two teams which trip feels slowest and note the answer.

title: Multiply to rank the journeys

beats.say: How do you decide which journey gets a paved road? You multiply.

Take how often a journey happens and how long it takes today. Publishing a batch data product is twenty a quarter at six weeks each. That is one hundred twenty weeks of waiting. Access requests are three hundred a quarter at four days each, about two hundred forty weeks.
A change data capture source adds thirty weeks. A streaming job adds thirty-two, but only four happen a quarter, so it can wait. The feature table adds four weeks. Skip it.

show.title: Decide
items: Pave now: access, batch publish, CDC

beats.say: Then shadow two teams doing the journey the hard way. Write down every wait, every question, every copy and paste. That list is your backlog.

check.q: Streaming jobs take eight weeks each, yet are paved later. Why?
opts: They happen only four times a quarter, so total pain is small
They are too complex for any platform team to ever pave
They are faster than batch jobs, so teams do not mind
They need no approval, so there is nothing to speed up
check.why: Ranking uses frequency times time. Four jobs a quarter gives modest total waiting, so streaming comes after journeys that hurt many more people.

work: Build your own table of journeys with count per quarter and time today.
Multiply the two columns and sort to get a first ranking.
Book shadow sessions with two teams for the top journey.

title: Traps when choosing journeys

beats.say: Why would a four day wait be paved before an eight week job?

Because volume wins. Access requests happen three hundred times a quarter. Streaming jobs happen four. And you keep the approval step. Self-service means the request is automatic, with a person approving only where the risk needs it.
Second trap: the time today column can mislead. Six weeks may be queues and handoffs, not real work. Shadow two teams so you pave the actual waits, not your guess.

show.title: Measure the real wait
items: Shadow two teams the hard way

beats.say: Third trap: ten thin paths. Each needs an owner, docs and upgrades. Spread thin, they rot, and teams drift back to the hard way. Do one or two well.

show.sub: Thin paths rot and get skipped

check.q: What does self-service mean for dataset access requests?
opts: Requests flow automatically and people approve only risky ones
Anyone gets any dataset instantly with no approval at all
Teams email owners directly but get a template for wording
The platform team approves every request faster than before
check.why: Self-service removes manual routing and waiting while keeping governance. Policy handles low-risk requests, and an owner approves only where the data is sensitive.

work: Split the last 50 access requests into those policy could approve and those needing a person.
Compare elapsed time with real effort for your slowest journey.

title: When not to pave

beats.say: When is not paving the smart architect move?

show.text: When paving does not pay back

beats.say: Paving costs build time and a standing owner. Suppose the batch path cuts six weeks to one. Twenty journeys a quarter then save a hundred team-weeks. That pays for a small team fast.

A feature table twice a quarter never pays back. Leave it unpaved, with good docs and office hours. Streaming waits until volume grows or the pattern settles, because paving a moving target means rebuilding it.

show.title: Leave unpaved on purpose
items: Rare one-offs: docs and office hours
Streaming: wait for volume and a stable pattern
Moving targets get rebuilt, wasting the paving

beats.say: Measure choice, not mandate. Track adoption and time to first publish each quarter, and re-rank the list. If teams skip the road, the road is wrong.

show.title: Quarterly loop
items: Track adoption and time to publish
Fix the path or pave the next

check.q: Teams keep avoiding a new paved path. What is the best reading?
opts: The path is worse than the hard way, so fix it
The teams are resisting change, so mandate the path
The journey is too rare, so remove the path docs
The adoption metric is flawed, so stop tracking it
check.why: Paved roads are chosen, not forced. Low adoption is a signal that the path costs more than the hard way, so improve it using what you learn from watching teams.

work: Estimate the weeks saved per quarter for your top journey before asking for headcount.
Pick adoption and time to first publish as the two metrics and review them quarterly.
Write a short note for unpaved journeys pointing to docs and office hours.

title: A paved road to production

beats.say: Thirty teams need to reach the same place. Why would each one build its own road?
Picture a town where every family paves a private route to the market. Each route works. But when a family is away, nobody else knows the turns, the bridges or the potholes.

chip.text: Only the builder knows the route

beats.say: A golden path is a road the town builds once. It is the easiest way to the market, and a crew keeps it repaired.
You may still cut across the field if you have a good reason. But then you carry your own boots, and your own repairs.

show.title: Optional, with a price
items: Off the road, you own the repairs

beats.say: In data, the market is a working pipeline. The road bundles the layout, tests, deployment and alerts, so nobody starts from a blank field.

check.q: What best describes a golden path?
opts: A supported, easiest way to do a common job that teams may leave
A required standard that every team must follow without exception
A shared document listing the tools that teams could consider
A one time starter project that teams then maintain on their own
check.why: A golden path is supported and easiest, but optional. Teams can leave for a good reason, and then they own what they build.

work: List the jobs your teams repeat most, such as starting a pipeline or adding alerts.
Ask three teams how they set up their last pipeline and note what differed.
Pick one repeated job as the first candidate for a paved road.

title: How a template becomes production in an hour

beats.say: How does a new pipeline reach production in one hour instead of one month?

show.sub: Decisions made once, reused many times

beats.say: A team picks the template and answers a few questions, like name, owner and schedule. The platform then generates a repository with the folder layout, a data contract file, test stubs, a deploy pipeline and alert rules.
Every decision that most teams should not debate is already made. The tool is chosen, tests run on every change, and ownership metadata is filled in, so the catalog and on call rota know who to page.
Three properties make it golden. It is the easiest way. The platform team supports and upgrades it. And it is optional, so it wins by being better, not by being forced.

check.q: Why can a template get a team to production in an hour?
opts: Common decisions on layout, tests, deploy and alerts are already made
Teams skip testing and monitoring until after the first release
The platform team writes each pipeline's business logic for them
Every team must use the same tool, which removes all choices
check.why: The speed comes from decisions being made once and generated for each team, not from skipping steps or writing their logic.

work: Write down the checklist a new pipeline needs before it counts as production ready.
Time how long your last new pipeline took from idea to first alert.
Draft the five questions a template should ask a team up front.

title: When the path drifts, stalls or becomes a cage

beats.say: You generated a pipeline from the template last year. Then the template improved. Did your pipeline get better?

Usually not. A copied template drifts. After a year you may have 30 repositories on 30 slightly different versions. So good paths ship upgrades as versioned libraries or automated pull requests, not just a one time copy.

A second failure is the path that fits only the common case. If it blocks a streaming job or a big backfill, teams leave, and that is fine. The signal to watch is why they leave. Count exits and fix the top reason.

show.title: Exits are a signal
items: Teams leave, and that is allowed

beats.say: The third failure is quiet mandates. If leaving the path needs executive sign off, it is no longer optional, and you lose the honest feedback that keeps it good. Off the path, the team owns its own on call and upgrades.

show.title: Keep it truly optional
items: Sign off to leave means a mandate
Off path means you own on call and upgrades

check.q: A year after launch, teams run many old versions of the template. What is the best fix?
opts: Ship upgrades as versioned libraries or automated pull requests
Tell teams to regenerate their repositories by hand each quarter
Freeze the template so that every repository stays identical
Require sign off for any team still on an older version
check.why: Copies drift once generated. Automated upgrades keep existing repositories current without forcing manual rework or a mandate.

work: Check how many repositories run each version of your template today.
Set up an automated pull request that bumps the shared library version.
Log the reason whenever a team leaves the path, and review the list monthly.

title: Is a golden path worth a platform team's year?

beats.say: When is a golden path a waste of a platform team's year?

show.text: When is it not worth it?
show.sub: Cost is fixed, savings scale with teams

beats.say: With three teams and one pipeline shape, a shared example repository is enough. A path pays off when many teams repeat the same job, say ten or more, because the cost of building it is fixed and the saving is multiplied by every team.
The hidden cost is upkeep. Every path is a product with users, a roadmap and support. Budget a standing team, and limit yourself to a few paths, such as batch and streaming, rather than one per team.

show.title: Paths are products
items: A standing team to run it
A few paths, not one per team

beats.say: Measure it like a product. Track adoption, time to first production run, and the share of pipelines off the path. If adoption is low, find the friction and fix it, do not mandate. Mandate only the few controls that law or security demand.

show.title: Measure and mandate sparingly
items: Mandate only legal and security controls

check.q: Adoption of your golden path is low after six months. What should you do first?
opts: Interview teams, find the friction, and fix the path itself
Mandate the path for all teams so adoption numbers rise quickly
Add more paths so that every team has its own tailored one
Remove the support team since few teams are using the path
check.why: Paths win by being better. Low adoption means friction. Mandates hide that signal, and more paths add upkeep cost.

work: Count how many teams repeat each job and rank candidates for a path by that number.
Set up a dashboard for adoption, time to first production run and off path share.
Separate the few mandatory controls from the optional conveniences in your platform.

title: The recipe card that drifts

beats.say: What happens to a recipe card after you photocopy it for eighty friends?
Each friend scribbles changes. A year later, you find a mistake: too much salt. You fix your own card, but the eighty copies stay wrong.
A software template works the same way. Teams copy it once to start a project, then it drifts away from the original.
The fix is to treat the template like a product. Give it version numbers, write down which version each copy came from, and send updates to every owner.
Better still, keep as little as possible in the copy. Point to a shared recipe instead of copying it.

check.q: Why does a fix to a template not reach projects already created from it?
opts: Each project holds its own copy, so changes to the original are not passed on
Projects always lock the template and refuse any later changes at all
Template fixes only apply to projects created on the same calendar day
check.why: A template is copied once. After that the copy is independent, so the original's fixes never reach it unless you send them on purpose.

work: Pick one template and list how many repositories came from it.
Ask whether each copied file could be shared instead of copied.

title: Upgrading eighty repositories

beats.say: How do you fix one security bug in eighty repositories?

show.sub: Without a plan, that is 80 manual edits

beats.say: First, version the template. Patch for fixes, minor for new optional pieces, major for changes owners must act on. Say it is version two point three point one.
Second, each repository records its starting version in a file the platform can read. Now a bot can tell which ones are behind.
Third, the bot opens an upgrade pull request in each one, with the diff and release notes. Owners review and merge. Nobody edits eighty repositories by hand.
A drift report ranks repositories by versions behind, so you chase the major-behind ones first.

check.q: What lets an upgrade bot know which repositories are behind the template?
opts: Each repository records the template version it was created from
The bot guesses by comparing repository names to the template name
Owners send the platform a message after every template release
check.why: A recorded version in a readable file lets the platform compare each repository with the latest release and compute how far behind it is.

work: Add a template version file to the template and to existing repositories.
Set up a bot that opens upgrade pull requests with release notes.

title: Why upgrades stall

beats.say: Why does an automated upgrade pull request still sit unmerged for months?

show.sub: A bot can propose. It cannot make owners act.

beats.say: Because the repository has drifted. The owner edited the copied files, so the bot's diff conflicts with their changes, and merging feels risky.
Major versions make it worse. They need owner action, so a bot cannot just merge them. Without a deprecation date, old versions live forever.
A drift report shows how many versions behind each repository is, and which files differ from the template. Without a recorded version, you cannot even compute that.
Also watch the bot's noise. Eighty pull requests with no release notes get ignored. Keep each change small and explained.

show.sub: Release notes make a merge safe

check.q: Why do upgrade pull requests often stall in repositories that edited the copied files?
opts: The owner's local edits conflict with the diff, so merging looks risky
The bot refuses to open requests for repositories with any local edits
Pull requests expire after a week and must be recreated by the owner
check.why: Copied files that were edited no longer match the template, so the diff conflicts or may overwrite local work. Owners then delay the merge.

work: Check the oldest open upgrade pull request and find why it is stuck.
Put a deprecation date on every old major version.

title: Share, don't copy

beats.say: Should every shared thing be a copied template file?

show.sub: Every copied file is a file to upgrade 80 times

beats.say: No. Every copied file is a file you must upgrade eighty times. For CI steps and deployment, use shared workflows or libraries. One change reaches everyone.
The trade-off is blast radius. A bad shared update breaks all eighty at once, so pin versions and roll out in waves.
Keep the template for what truly must be owned per repository: names, service code, config. Keep it thin.
Then run it like a product. Publish deprecation dates, track drift, and measure the share of repositories on the latest version.

check.q: For CI steps used by eighty repositories, what is the best default?
opts: A shared workflow that every repository calls and you update in one place
A copied file in every repository, with a bot sending upgrade pull requests
A wiki page that tells each team how to update its own CI steps
check.why: Sharing means one change reaches everyone with no per-repository upgrade. Copies need eighty upgrades. Pin versions to limit the blast radius.

work: List the copied files in your template and move shared logic into libraries or shared workflows.
Add a staged rollout and rollback plan for shared updates.
Publish a drift dashboard and review it monthly.

title: The front desk for your platform

beats.say: Ever walked into a huge building with no reception desk, and no idea where anything is?

show.sub: A huge building, and no map

beats.say: A developer portal is that front desk for a company's data and software. It holds a map of everything, a note of who owns each room, and the instructions pinned next to each door.
It also has order forms. Want a new data pipeline? Fill in a short form, and the portal builds it the approved way. Like choosing a ready-made kitchen instead of designing one from scratch.
Finally, it has report cards. They show which rooms meet the safety rules, and which need fixing. One front door means nobody wanders around guessing.

show.title: Why one front door wins
items: A named owner for each part
Report cards show what needs fixing

check.q: What is the main job of a developer portal?
opts: Give people one front door to find, create, and check things
Run every pipeline so that the scheduler is not needed
Store all the company's raw data in a single place
Replace the engineers who would otherwise build things
check.why: The portal is a front door: it lists what exists, creates new components from templates, and shows how each meets standards. It does not run pipelines or hold the data.

work: Write down where a new joiner would look today to find who owns a pipeline.
List the three questions people ask most often in chat that a front desk could answer.

title: Catalog, templates, scorecards: the moving parts

beats.say: A team has forty pipelines. How do you find the owner of one at three in the morning?

show.sub: Who owns this one, right now?

beats.say: The portal's catalog answers it. Each component has a small metadata file in its own repository, naming the owner, the type, and what it depends on. The portal reads those files on a schedule, often every few minutes, and draws the graph.
Templates use the same trick in reverse. A short form asks for a name, an owner, and a source. The portal then creates a repository with pipeline code, tests, a contract, and a metadata file.
Scorecards then check each component against rules, such as has an owner, tests pass, and on the latest template version. A score of eight out of ten tells a team exactly what to fix.

check.q: How does the catalog usually learn that a pipeline exists and who owns it?
opts: Engineers retype every entry into the portal by hand
It reads a metadata file kept in each component's repository
It scans the warehouse tables and guesses the owner from names
A central team interviews every team once per quarter
check.why: Each repository carries a small metadata file naming the owner, type, and dependencies. The portal reads these on a schedule, so the catalog follows the code.

work: Pick one pipeline and write the metadata it would need: owner, type, and dependencies.
Choose three scorecard checks you could measure automatically today.

title: Where portals go wrong

beats.say: Why does the portal say a pipeline is healthy when it died last week?
Because a catalog is only as fresh as its sources. Metadata files are written by hand, so they rot. Owners leave, teams rename, and the entry still points at a person who quit.
The fix is to pull facts from live systems, like the scheduler and the warehouse, and check that every owner still exists in the directory. Hand-written fields should be the exception.
Scorecards have a trap too. Once a score is a target, teams game it. They add an empty contract just to turn the check green. Score what matters, like passing tests and met SLOs, not just presence.

show.title: Scorecard traps
items: Empty contract turns the check green
Score tests passing and SLOs met

beats.say: Last, two catalogs split trust. Let the portal link to the data catalog, or show its data products, never copy them by hand.

check.q: A scorecard shows green for every contract check, yet consumers still get broken data. What is the likely cause?
opts: The portal is reading the repositories too often
Backstage cannot display more than a few dozen checks
The check tests that a contract exists, not that it is enforced
Data products should not have owners listed in the catalog
check.why: Presence checks are easy to game. An empty or unenforced contract passes, so scorecards should measure outcomes such as tests passing and SLOs met.

work: Audit ten catalog entries and count how many owners no longer exist.
Replace one presence check with an outcome check, like freshness SLO met.

title: Is a portal worth building?

beats.say: Is a developer portal worth a full-time team?

Backstage is free to download but not free to run. Expect two to four engineers to maintain plugins, upgrades, and ingestion. Below about fifty engineers, a well-kept wiki page and a repository template list often does the job.

Past a few hundred engineers, discovery and ownership gaps cost more. Then weigh buying a hosted portal against building on Backstage. Buying trades flexibility for speed; building lets you model data products your way.
Whatever you choose, keep one source of truth for data. The data catalog owns lineage and schemas. The portal owns templates and scorecards, and links across.
Adoption is the real metric. If teams only use the portal because they must, the golden path is a mandate, not a road they choose.

show.sub: A road teams choose, not a mandate

check.q: A company of thirty engineers is considering Backstage. What is the best advice?
opts: Start with Backstage now, since portals only work if built early
Buy two portals so that data and software each get their own
Keep a simple wiki and templates, and revisit as headcount grows
Skip owners and scorecards, because small teams never need them
check.why: A self-hosted portal needs a few engineers to run. At thirty engineers, a wiki and repository templates give most of the value at far lower cost.

work: Estimate the yearly cost of running a portal against the hours lost searching for owners.
Decide which system is the source of truth for each fact, and write it down.
Track how many teams pick the template without being told to.

title: A guardrail beats a guard

beats.say: Why do mountain roads have guardrails instead of a guard who checks every car?

show.sub: Which one keeps a busy road moving?

beats.say: A gate is a person. Every driver stops, waits for approval, and soon finds a side road around it. A guardrail is just there. It catches you when you drift, and nobody has to be asked.

show.title: A *gate* waits, a rail just works

chip.text: Waiting teaches people to dodge you

beats.say: Data teams work the same way. If a computer checks that personal details are hidden, the team gets an answer in seconds, with the fix spelled out.
And when someone truly must cross, there is a pass. It has a name, a reason and an end date.

show.title: A pass, not a hole
items: A reason: why it is needed
An end date: when it is revisited

check.q: Why do guardrails usually work better than a person who approves every change?
opts: They answer instantly and consistently, so teams have no reason to dodge them
They are cheaper because they never need any rules to be written down
They make sure that no team ever needs an exception to any rule
They let teams skip testing since the rail will catch every mistake
check.why: A guardrail gives an instant, same-every-time answer with a fix. Waiting on a person pushes teams to route around you. Rules still need writing, exceptions still happen, and tests still matter.

work: List the approvals teams wait on today and mark which could be an automatic check.
Pick one approval and write the rule it enforces in one plain sentence.

title: Five checks, two minutes

beats.say: How can a check replace a review board and still catch mistakes?

show.text: Replace the meeting with a pipeline

beats.say: A team opens a pull request for a new data product. A pipeline runs five checks automatically. Contract exists and matches the data. Personal columns are tagged and masked. An owner and on-call channel are named. Tests pass. Cost fits the quota.

show.title: The five checks
items: Contract exists and data matches it

beats.say: Each failure prints the exact fix, such as: column email is untagged, add the pii tag. The whole run takes about two minutes. A review ticket often sat for three days.
Same rules, every team, every time. People now only design the rules, not police each change.

check.q: A check fails because a column called email has no personal data tag. What makes the guardrail useful here?
opts: It tells the team the exact fix, so they can correct it within minutes
It quietly tags the column for them and lets the release continue
It sends the pull request to a board that meets weekly to decide
It records the failure for a later audit and lets the release go ahead
check.why: A guardrail stops the mistake and explains how to fix it, so the loop is minutes. Silent auto-fixing, a weekly board, or just logging for later all fail to give that fast, clear feedback.

work: Write each of your data rules as a check that prints a one-line fix message.
Measure how long a new data product takes to get a yes or no today, and set a target under ten minutes.

title: When guardrails go wrong

beats.say: What happens when a guardrail is wrong, or a team truly cannot comply?

show.text: What if the rule is wrong?
show.sub: Every check needs a way out

beats.say: That needs an escape hatch: a waiver with a reason, an owner and an expiry date, stored where the check itself can read it. No expiry means a permanent hole. With expiry, a shortcut becomes a dated decision someone must revisit.

chip.text: No expiry means a permanent hole

beats.say: Watch for flaky checks. If a guardrail blocks good work one time in ten, teams stop trusting it and ask for a bypass. Also, a check that runs only at deploy misses drift, like a new unmasked column arriving next month. So quality checks must run in production too.

show.title: Failure modes
items: Flaky check: trust drains, bypass requests rise
Fix: run quality checks in production too

beats.say: Roll out new rules in warn mode first, then block.

check.q: A masking check passed at deploy. Next month a new unmasked column appears in production. What went wrong?
opts: The check only ran at deploy, so later drift in production was never seen
The waiver for the check had no owner, so the pipeline skipped masking
The contract was too strict, which made teams add columns in secret
The check was set to block, which taught teams to bypass the pipeline
check.why: Deploy-time checks cannot see change that arrives later. Production checks catch drift. Missing waiver owners, strict contracts, or blocking mode do not explain a column appearing after a pass.

work: Add an expiry date and owner field to every waiver, and make the check fail on expired ones.
Start each new rule in warn mode and track its false alarm rate before blocking.

title: When to keep a gate

beats.say: If guardrails are so good, should you ever keep a human gate?

show.text: Is a human gate ever right?

beats.say: Yes, when a mistake is costly and cannot be undone, like sharing regulated data outside the company. A person should look at that. Reversible, common mistakes, like a missing owner, belong to automation.

show.title: Match the control to the *blast radius*

chip.text: Gate only what you cannot undo

beats.say: Guardrails are not free. Someone owns the rules, the fix messages and the false positives. Start by blocking only high-risk failures, and warn on the rest. Track three numbers: share of products passing first time, open waivers, and days to expiry.

show.title: Run guardrails like a product
items: Block high risk, warn on the rest
Track open waivers and days to expiry

beats.say: A rising waiver count means the rule is wrong or the paved road is too narrow. Fix that, not the team.

show.sub: Fix the rule or widen the road

check.q: Waivers for one rule keep climbing across many teams. What is the best reading of this?
opts: The rule or the paved road does not fit real needs, so redesign it
The teams are careless, so the rule should move to a human gate
The expiry dates are too short, so they should be removed entirely
The check is working well, since teams use the waiver process often
check.why: Widespread waivers signal a mismatch between the rule and real work, so fix the rule or the road. Blaming teams, removing expiry, or treating high waiver volume as success all hide the signal.

work: Report waiver count per rule monthly and review the top offender.
Classify each approval as reversible or irreversible, and keep a human gate only for the irreversible ones.
Assign an owner to each guardrail for rules, messages and false positives.

title: Is anyone using the new road?

beats.say: You built a shiny new highway. How do you know anyone actually drives on it?

chip.text: Built is not the same as used

beats.say: A city does not just open a road and cheer. It counts the cars. That count is adoption: out of all new trips, how many take the road? It also times the trip. If the old back lane is faster, drivers keep using the lane.
Then it counts crashes and help calls, and asks drivers a few questions. If few people use the road, the city asks why before banning the back lane. Maybe the road misses a town people need to reach.

show.title: What a city checks
items: Ask before you ban the lane

check.q: Few drivers use your new highway. What should the city do first?
opts: Ask drivers why, since the road may miss a place they need
Close the back lane so drivers have no other choice
Build a second highway beside the first one right away
Wait a year, because low use always fixes itself over time
check.why: Low use is a signal. The road may not reach a real destination or may be slower. Forcing drivers hides that problem and builds resentment.

work: List which teams skipped your standard path and ask one of them why.
Write down the old way people use and time it against the path.

title: The six numbers of a golden path

beats.say: Your team built a pipeline template. Is it working, or just sitting there?

show.sub: Measure the path like a product

beats.say: Adoption is new pipelines on the path divided by all new pipelines. Say eighteen of thirty this quarter: sixty percent. Then time to first production run. Maybe three days on the path, against fifteen days off it.

Next, delivery health for repositories on the path. Lead time for changes is how long a change takes to reach production. Change failure rate is the share of deploys that cause a problem. Compare both with off-path repositories.
Add support tickets per project, and a short quarterly survey. Ask people who left the path why they left. Also track drift: the share of repositories on a supported template version.

show.title: The rest of the scorecard
items: Drift: share on a supported version

check.q: Eighteen of thirty new pipelines this quarter used the template. What does that number tell you?
opts: Adoption is sixty percent, which says people choose the path
Drift is sixty percent, which says templates are up to date
Failure rate is sixty percent, which says the path is risky
Satisfaction is sixty percent, which says users are happy
check.why: Adoption is new pipelines on the path over all new pipelines. It says nothing about drift, failures or satisfaction, which need their own measures.

work: Pull the count of new pipelines per quarter and how many used the template.
Measure days to first production run for one on-path and one off-path team.

title: When good numbers lie

beats.say: Adoption hit ninety percent. Is the path a success?
Not necessarily. If the path was mandated, people comply, they do not choose. Watch support tickets and survey answers. High adoption with rising tickets means people are suffering on the path.
Beware selection bias. Strong teams may join the path first, so faster delivery may reflect the team, not the path. Compare the same team before and after, or teams of similar size and skill.

show.title: A fair comparison
items: Do not credit the path for strong teams

beats.say: Then drift. A repository that copied the template two years ago is on the path in name only, and misses every fix since. Count the template version, not just whether the template was used.

check.q: A team claims the path speeds up delivery because on-path repos ship faster. What is the main risk in that claim?
opts: Strong teams may have joined first, so the path gets undeserved credit
Faster shipping always means a higher change failure rate
Repos on the path cannot be compared with any other repos
Lead time only counts when drift is exactly zero percent
check.why: Selection bias confuses team strength with path benefit. A before and after view, or a comparison of similar teams, gives a fairer answer.

work: Check how many repos run a template version that is no longer supported.
Compare lead time for the same teams before and after they moved to the path.

title: Low adoption: fix it, mandate it, or retire it

beats.say: Adoption is low. Do you mandate the path?
Not first. Ask why. Usually the path misses a real need, or it is slower than the old way. A mandate hides that gap and buys resentment, and teams will build workarounds anyway.

chip.text: Fix the path, not the people

beats.say: Pick a few metrics: adoption, time to first run, drift. Collect them automatically from repository and pipeline metadata. Keep surveys short and quarterly. Never rank teams with these numbers, because people will game them.

show.title: Keep measurement cheap
items: Collected from repo and CI data

beats.say: With only three teams, skip dashboards and just talk to them. And if a path stays unused after you fix it, retire it. Maintaining it costs real engineers.

check.q: Adoption of your path stays at twenty percent. What is the best first step as an architect?
opts: Interview the teams who left to find the gap or slowness
Mandate the path now and track compliance in a dashboard
Add more metrics to the dashboard until the cause shows up
Rank teams by adoption so peer pressure raises the number
check.why: Low adoption usually means the path misses a need or is slower than the old way. Learning that first lets you fix the cause instead of forcing compliance.

work: Interview two teams that left the path and write down the top reason.
Choose three core metrics and automate their collection from repo data.

title: The road people choose

beats.say: Why do some company roads sit empty while everyone walks through the grass?

show.sub: Why do teams skip the paved path?

beats.say: A golden path is a paved road for building data pipelines. Teams choose it because it is faster, not because they are forced. Fence it in with no exits, and people climb the fence. That is a golden cage.
Build ten roads and fix none, and every road has potholes. Build a road without asking walkers where they go, and it stays empty.
Put a toll booth at the end, where you must file a ticket, and it is a gate wearing a road costume. Skip the signs, and nobody can fix a breakdown. Good roads are few, current, open, and understood.

check.q: A company makes its pipeline template mandatory with no way to change it. Teams start working around it. What failure is this?
opts: A golden cage, because a path that cannot bend gets fought
Stale templates, because old versions are still in use
Too many paths, because teams have too many choices
A missing upgrade bot, because teams cannot get updates
check.why: A path nobody can leave pushes teams to fight it. Paved roads work when teams choose them because they are better, and can still step off when needed.

work: List the templates your platform offers and mark which ones teams actually use.
Ask one team where the current path forced a bad fit, and add an escape hatch for it.
Check whether any step of your path still ends in a ticket.

title: Keeping templates fresh and free

beats.say: A template fixed a security bug last week. Why are forty repositories still broken?
Because copying a template happens once. Each repository drifts from the day it is created. The cure is versioning. Every release gets a number, and every repository records which one it came from.
Then an upgrade bot opens a pull request in all forty repositories within minutes. A drift report lists who is behind, say twelve of forty, so owners can see it.
The same idea fixes approvals. A ticket to the platform team takes five days. An automatic check in the pipeline takes two minutes, and enforces the same rules.

check.q: Why does a versioned template with an upgrade bot beat a template that is simply copied once?
opts: Fixes can reach every repository as pull requests, not manual copying
Repositories can no longer change any code the template made
Teams never need to review changes made to their repositories
The template is only copied once, so storage costs stay lower
check.why: Recorded versions let a bot find every repository behind and open an upgrade pull request. Owners still review, but the work no longer depends on people remembering.

work: Make every generated repository record the template version it came from.
Turn on an upgrade bot and publish a weekly drift report.
Replace one approval ticket with an automatic pipeline check.

title: Where golden paths quietly break

beats.say: Your template has a hundred repositories. Is that success?

show.sub: Success, or a pile of future stale code?

beats.say: Not necessarily. Creation counts are vanity. Ask how many still deploy weekly and how many are on the latest version. A repository made once and abandoned is a stale template waiting to bite.

Upgrade bots also fail quietly. If tests are flaky, owners ignore the pull requests, and drift grows. Heavy edits to generated files cause merge conflicts, so logic should live in a shared library that updates by version number instead.

Escape hatches need care. Let teams leave the path, but keep automatic guardrails like access and cost checks on. And when generated defaults are opaque, nobody can debug them at three in the morning. Document how it works, with examples.

show.title: Open, but safe
items: Examples show how to debug it

check.q: Teams keep ignoring the upgrade pull requests, and repositories fall further behind. What is the most likely root cause to check first?
opts: Flaky tests make upgrades risky, so owners stop trusting them
The template version number is too high for repositories to use
Too many teams are using the one template that was supplied
The upgrade bot sends too few pull requests to be noticed
check.why: If tests fail randomly, owners cannot tell a good upgrade from a bad one and learn to ignore the bot. Reliable tests make upgrades safe to merge.

work: Track weekly deploys and version currency, not just repositories created.
Move shared logic out of generated files into a versioned library.
Write a short how-it-works page covering every default the template generates.

title: When to build a path, and when not to

beats.say: When should you not build a golden path?

show.text: When is a path the wrong tool?
show.sub: Every path has a running cost

beats.say: When only three teams exist, or each workload is truly unique. A path needs an owner, upgrades and support, often half an engineer or more per journey. That cost only pays back when many teams repeat the same work.
Before building, shadow two or three real teams for a week. Pick the one or two journeys they repeat most, like a batch pipeline or a streaming job. Ten thin paths lose to two good ones.

show.title: Start narrow
items: Pick the one or two most repeated journeys
Do them well before adding more

beats.say: Then measure adoption and time to first deploy as you would for a product. If teams avoid it, fix the path, not the mandate. Where variety is high, ship shared libraries and examples instead of a full template.

show.title: Treat the path as a product

check.q: Adoption of your pipeline template is low. As the platform architect, what is the best response?
opts: Find why teams avoid it and fix the path to earn adoption
Make the template mandatory so every team uses it right away
Add six more templates so every team finds one that fits it
Stop measuring adoption, since teams know what works for them
check.why: Low adoption is product feedback. A mandate creates a cage, and more templates spread upkeep thin. Learn the friction, then improve the path.

work: Shadow two teams for a week and write down the steps they repeat.
Cap active paths at two and name an owner for each.
Track adoption and time to first deploy on a simple dashboard.
